tip_title: Holiday Gifts Are Coming Into Your Home. Some of Them Might Already Be Under-Insured.
topic: Home Insurance - Personal Property Sub-Limits for High-Value Items
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Home Policy Has Sub-Limits on Specific Categories of Valuables**

Standard homeowners and renters policies cover personal property up to a total limit — but inside that limit, certain categories of items have their own sub-caps that kick in regardless of what the overall number says. Jewelry is a common one: many policies cap jewelry theft claims at $1,500 to $2,500 total, no matter how much your ring or watch is actually worth. Electronics, fine art, collectibles, and firearms often carry their own sub-limits too. The holiday season brings a lot of new, higher-value items into the house — and it's also when theft risk runs highest. If you're giving or receiving anything pricey this year, it's worth confirming what your policy actually covers for that category before something happens.

Your Peachy agent can walk you through what sub-limits are on your current policy and whether a scheduled personal property endorsement makes sense for specific items.

📖 [Learn more from Policygenius](https://www.policygenius.com/homeowners-insurance/actual-cash-value-vs-replacement-cost/)
summary: Covers personal property sub-limits within homeowners and renters policies for specific high-value categories (jewelry, electronics, fine art) framed as a holiday season check — distinct from prior tips on overall personal property limits and ACV vs. replacement cost settlement methods.
scoring_notes: Publishing Nov 27, peak holiday gift-giving season. Prior personal property tips covered ACV vs. replacement cost (Nov 6, Nov 23), overall personal property limits (Oct 26), and home inventory documentation — none covered the sub-limit mechanic specifically. This is a genuinely distinct and actionable concept that most readers have never encountered. Works across all three audiences: homeowners (78% East Cobb, 65% Lewisville Lake) and the 45% renters in Perimeter both have personal property sub-limits on their respective policies. Income levels across all three neighborhoods put jewelry, electronics, and holiday gift spending in realistic territory. Policygenius is on the trusted source list.

tip_title: More Miles, More Risk: What to Confirm on Your Auto Policy Before the Holiday Stretch
topic: Auto Insurance - Holiday Season Driving and Year-End Policy Review
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: The Holidays Mean More Driving. Make Sure Your Auto Coverage Is Ready.**

Thanksgiving weekend is statistically one of the busiest travel periods of the year, and December isn't much lighter. More cars on the road, fatigue from long drives, unfamiliar routes, and weather that can turn fast — it all adds up to elevated risk during exactly the stretch when most people aren't thinking about their insurance at all. Two things worth confirming before you log those extra miles: whether your bodily injury liability limits are adequate (the default minimums most people are carrying are lower than most people realize), and whether your policy lists all the drivers in your household who might be behind the wheel over the next five weeks.

Not sure where your limits land or whether everyone in your household is properly covered? Your Peachy agent can pull that up for you fast.

📖 [Learn more from NerdWallet](https://www.nerdwallet.com/insurance/auto/learn/usage-based-car-insurance)
summary: Covers auto insurance readiness for the Thanksgiving-through-December holiday travel stretch, specifically liability limit adequacy and ensuring all household drivers are listed on the policy, framed as a late-November action item before peak holiday road volume.
scoring_notes: Publishing on Nov 27, the Friday after Thanksgiving — peak holiday travel weekend. Auto liability limit adequacy was last covered Nov 13 (Thanksgiving travel angle focused on bodily injury per-occurrence limits and multi-person accident gap). This tip approaches from a different angle: the full five-week holiday stretch rather than just Thanksgiving, with the added household driver listing check as a distinct actionable item. Works across all three audiences — high homeownership doesn't reduce auto relevance, and the multi-driver household angle lands especially well for the family-heavy East Cobb and Lewisville Lake audiences. NerdWallet is on the trusted source list.

tip_title: December Is Three Weeks Out. When Did You Last Check Who Gets Your Life Insurance?
topic: Life Insurance - Year-End Beneficiary and Coverage Review
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Year-End Is the Right Time to Check Your Life Insurance Beneficiaries**

End of year is a natural reset point, and one thing worth five minutes of your time before January rolls in is pulling up your life insurance policy and confirming your beneficiary designations are still accurate. Life moves fast. A marriage, a divorce, the birth of a kid, the loss of a parent, a big birthday where the kids finally leave the house — any of those changes the picture. The person you named ten years ago might not be the right answer today, and beneficiary designations override your will, so the policy pays out to whoever's listed regardless of what your other documents say.

Not sure how to pull that info up or whether your coverage amount still makes sense for where you are now? Your Peachy agent can help you work through it quickly.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org)
summary: Covers year-end as a prompt to review life insurance beneficiary designations and confirm coverage amounts are still accurate after life changes — framed as a December reset action item rather than a purchase decision.
scoring_notes: Late November publish date makes year-end framing timely and natural. Life insurance beneficiary review was last covered June 14 (general beneficiary review) and the Oct 16 tip focused on coverage adequacy review — this tip combines both angles under a year-end reset frame that's distinctly seasonal. Crosses all three audiences: homeowners and renters alike, every income bracket, every age group represented. No candidate in the provided list covers this topic, so sourcing the III as a trusted evergreen reference is appropriate. Prior coverage-review tip (Oct 16) focused on how debts and income changes make existing amounts outdated; this tip centers on the beneficiary designation mechanic and the year-end calendar trigger as a fresh angle.
